en.title: The Organisation of African Unity is founded
en.text:
## Addis Ababa, 25 May 1963

In May 1963, the Ethiopian capital became the meeting place of a generation that had inherited newly independent states and an unfinished continental struggle. Thirty-two African heads of state and government gathered in Addis Ababa. They came from countries with different languages, political systems and colonial experiences, but they shared a pressing question: could the continent defend its new independence and shape a common future?

On 25 May they signed the Charter establishing the Organisation of African Unity (OAU). The date became a landmark in the history of Pan-Africanism and is now commemorated as Africa Day. The OAU was not a government for Africa. It was an organisation of sovereign states that agreed to cooperate while retaining their independence.

## A continent emerging from colonial rule

The OAU's creation followed decades of resistance to colonial domination. European powers had divided most of Africa among themselves during the late nineteenth century. Colonial borders cut across older political communities and trading networks, while colonial economies were generally organised to serve imperial interests.

The Second World War weakened European empires and strengthened demands for self-government. African political movements, trade unions, veterans, students, religious organisations and intellectuals challenged colonial rule. Independence came at different times and through different routes. Ghana became independent in 1957; Guinea followed in 1958; and a large wave of African countries gained independence in 1960.

Yet in 1963 much of the continent remained under colonial or minority rule. Algeria had only recently emerged from a devastating war of independence. Angola, Mozambique, Guinea-Bissau, Southern Rhodesia and South Africa remained central to the struggle against colonialism and white minority rule. Leaders understood that the freedom of one country would remain vulnerable while neighbouring peoples were still ruled by outside powers.

## The Pan-African idea

The OAU was the institutional expression of a much older Pan-African idea: that people of African descent and African societies shared interests that could not be protected by isolated states alone. The movement had developed through intellectual, political and cultural networks linking Africa, the Caribbean, Europe and the Americas.

In the twentieth century, figures such as W.E.B. Du Bois, Marcus Garvey, George Padmore and Kwame Nkrumah helped make Pan-Africanism a political programme. Nkrumah, Ghana's first prime minister and later president, argued that political independence would be incomplete unless African states worked together. He warned that small, economically dependent states could remain vulnerable to external pressure.

Other leaders favoured a more gradual approach. They wanted cooperation but were cautious about surrendering sovereignty to a continental federation. This disagreement shaped the diplomacy that led to the OAU.

## Casablanca and Monrovia: two approaches to unity

Before the Addis Ababa summit, African governments had debated how unity should work. The Casablanca Group, which included Ghana, Guinea, Mali, Morocco, Egypt and Algeria, supported stronger political coordination and a more ambitious form of African unity. Some of its members favoured institutions that could eventually move beyond cooperation among governments.

The Monrovia Group, which included Nigeria, Liberia, Senegal, Ethiopia and others, placed greater emphasis on the sovereignty of existing states, non-interference and practical cooperation. Its members feared that a rapid federation could create new conflicts or allow powerful states to dominate smaller ones.

These were not simply arguments between people who wanted unity and people who opposed it. Both groups supported African cooperation, but disagreed about its pace, institutions and limits. The Addis Ababa negotiations produced a compromise: a continental organisation built around independent member states.

## The founding summit

Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia hosted the summit in Addis Ababa. The leaders who attended included Nkrumah of Ghana, Nyerere of Tanganyika, Sekou Touré of Guinea, Ahmed Ben Bella of Algeria, Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt and many others.

Their discussions were difficult. They had to agree on the meaning of sovereignty, how disputes between states should be handled, how liberation movements could be supported and how cooperation could be organised without creating a central authority that member governments would reject.

The Charter was signed on 25 May 1963. It established the Organisation of African Unity and set out its purposes. These included promoting unity and solidarity, coordinating cooperation for development, defending the sovereignty and territorial integrity of member states, eradicating colonialism and promoting international cooperation.

The Charter also affirmed principles that reflected the compromise among the founders: sovereign equality of member states, respect for territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. The principles helped reassure governments that the new organisation would not simply become an instrument for one state to control another.

## Liberation as a continental responsibility

One of the OAU's most important roles was to keep the liberation of the remaining dependent territories on the continental agenda. The organisation created a Liberation Committee, based in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, to coordinate assistance to movements fighting colonial and minority rule.

The committee became an important centre for diplomatic and material support. Newly independent states provided political backing, training opportunities, funds and other assistance to liberation movements. Tanzania, under Julius Nyerere, became a particularly important base for several movements from southern Africa.

The OAU also used international diplomacy. Member states raised colonialism and apartheid in the United Nations and other international forums. Their collective voice helped make African liberation a central issue in world politics.

The struggle was not straightforward. African governments differed over which movements to support, how to respond to armed struggle and how to deal with neighbouring states that cooperated with colonial regimes. Nevertheless, the OAU gave the continent a permanent platform from which to challenge colonial rule.

## Cooperation and its limitations

The organisation's ambitions extended beyond liberation. Its Charter called for cooperation in politics, diplomacy, economics, transport, communications, education, culture, health, science, technology, defence and security.

In practice, progress was uneven. Many member states had limited financial resources and weak transport links inherited from colonial rule. Their economies often depended on exporting a small number of raw materials. Differences in language, political ideology and national priorities made joint projects difficult.

The OAU also faced a fundamental contradiction. It defended the sovereignty of governments, including governments that came to power through coups or ruled without meaningful political competition. Its commitment to non-interference could make it difficult to respond decisively to abuses within member states. The organisation was often more effective at defending states from external domination than at protecting citizens from their own governments.

Border disputes and interstate conflicts also tested the principle of peaceful settlement. The OAU helped create diplomatic channels and supported the principle that colonial-era borders should generally be respected, partly to avoid a continent-wide wave of territorial wars. That approach reduced one source of potential conflict, although it did not resolve every dispute.

## From the OAU to the African Union

By the end of the twentieth century, African leaders increasingly argued that the OAU needed stronger institutions to address economic integration, conflict prevention and the changing global economy. The end of apartheid and the political transformation of South Africa also changed the continental environment.

The Constitutive Act of the African Union was adopted in 2000. The African Union was officially launched in Durban, South Africa, in July 2002, succeeding the OAU. The AU retained the Pan-African ambition of its predecessor but established new institutions and gave greater attention to integration, peace and security, democratic governance and development.

The change did not mean that the OAU's history had become irrelevant. The AU inherited its achievements, unresolved debates and institutional legacy. The OAU had helped consolidate the principle that African states should act together against colonial domination. The AU sought to build a more capable organisation for a different era.

## Why 25 May still matters

Africa Day recalls the decision made in Addis Ababa in 1963. It is a celebration of political solidarity, but it is also an opportunity to examine how far the continent has travelled toward the goals written into the Charter.

The founders wanted freedom, dignity, cooperation and control over Africa's future. Their organisation helped coordinate the final stages of decolonisation and gave African governments a collective diplomatic voice. It did not create the united political and economic system imagined by the most ambitious Pan-Africanists, and it struggled to respond to conflicts and abuses within member states.

The OAU's history is therefore both an achievement and an unfinished project. Its creation marked a moment when newly independent governments chose to build a continental institution rather than face the world separately. The African Union continues that work, while the questions debated in 1963—sovereignty, solidarity, development and the meaning of unity—remain central to African politics.

## Key people

Kwame Nkrumah: Ghanaian leader and a prominent advocate of continental political unity.

Haile Selassie: Emperor of Ethiopia and host of the 1963 Addis Ababa summit.

Julius Nyerere: President of Tanganyika and later Tanzania; a supporter of African liberation and regional cooperation.

Sekou Touré: President of Guinea and an influential Pan-African voice.

Gamal Abdel Nasser: President of Egypt and one of the prominent leaders involved in African and Arab political cooperation.

## Timeline

1957: Ghana becomes independent, strengthening the momentum for African decolonisation.

1958: The All-African Peoples' Conference meets in Accra.

1960: A major wave of African countries gains independence.

1961: The Casablanca Group advances proposals for stronger African political unity.

1962: The Monrovia Group promotes cooperation that preserves state sovereignty.

25 May 1963: Thirty-two independent African states sign the OAU Charter in Addis Ababa.

1963: The OAU Liberation Committee is established to coordinate support for liberation movements.

1990: Namibia becomes independent, marking a major late achievement in African decolonisation.

1994: Apartheid ends as South Africa holds its first democratic election.

2000: The Constitutive Act of the African Union is adopted.

July 2002: The African Union is officially launched in Durban, succeeding the OAU.

## Sources

African Union, “About the African Union” and its institutional history.

United Nations Treaty Series, Charter of the Organisation of African Unity, signed at Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963, vol. 479, No. 6947.

African Union, OAU Charter and historical documents on the founding organisation.

fr.title: Fondation de l'Organisation de l'unité africaine (OUA)
fr.text: Les dirigeants des États africains indépendants fondent l'OUA, ancêtre de l'Union africaine (UA). Cette date est aujourd'hui célébrée comme la Journée de l'Afrique.

ar.title: تأسيس منظمة الوحدة الأفريقية
ar.text: أسس قادة الدول الأفريقية المستقلة منظمة الوحدة الأفريقية، التي سبقت الاتحاد الأفريقي. ويُحتفل بهذا التاريخ اليوم باسم يوم أفريقيا.

ko.title: 아프리카 통일기구(OAU) 창설
ko.text: 독립한 아프리카 국가들의 지도자들이 아프리카연합(AU)의 전신인 OAU를 창설했습니다. 이날은 오늘날 아프리카의 날로 기념됩니다.

ja.title: アフリカ統一機構(OAU)の設立
ja.place: エチオピア・アディスアベバ
ja.text: 独立したアフリカ諸国の指導者たちが、アフリカ連合(AU)の前身であるOAUを設立しました。この日は現在「アフリカの日」として祝われています。

zh.title: 非洲统一组织(OAU)成立
zh.place: 埃塞俄比亚亚的斯亚贝巴
zh.text: 独立的非洲国家领导人成立了非洲统一组织,即非洲联盟(AU)的前身。这一天如今被定为“非洲日”。

es.title: Fundación de la Organización para la Unidad Africana (OUA)
es.text: Los líderes de los Estados africanos independientes fundaron la OUA, predecesora de la Unión Africana (UA). Esta fecha se celebra hoy como el Día de África.

sw.title: Kuanzishwa kwa Umoja wa Nchi Huru za Afrika (OAU)
sw.text: Viongozi wa nchi huru za Afrika walianzisha OAU, chombo kilichotangulia Umoja wa Afrika (AU). Tarehe hii sasa huadhimishwa kama Siku ya Afrika.

en.title: Nelson Mandela is released
en.place: Paarl and Cape Town, South Africa
en.text:
## The gates at Victor Verster

On Sunday, 11 February 1990, Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela walked out of Victor Verster Prison near Paarl in South Africa's Western Cape. He had spent more than twenty-seven years in prison. Waiting crowds and international television cameras watched as he emerged beside his wife, Winnie Madikizela-Mandela, and raised his fist.

The moment became one of the most recognisable images of the twentieth century. It was not the end of South Africa's struggle against apartheid. It was the beginning of a new and uncertain phase: negotiations over how a country built on racial domination could become a democracy.

Mandela was 71 years old. He had entered prison as a leading opponent of white minority rule and emerged as a central figure in negotiations that would reshape South Africa.

## A country divided by law

Apartheid was a system of racial segregation and white political control developed under the National Party government after it came to power in 1948. It built on earlier colonial and segregationist laws, but made racial classification and separation more comprehensive.

The state classified people into racial categories and used those categories to determine where they could live, work, study and travel. The Group Areas Act assigned residential areas by race. Pass laws restricted the movement of Black South Africans. The Bantu Education system provided an unequal education designed to prepare Black people for a subordinate position in society. Political representation and access to land, jobs and public services were also structured by race.

Resistance existed long before Mandela became internationally known. Workers, rural communities, women, students, churches, trade unions and political organisations challenged dispossession and discrimination. The African National Congress (ANC), founded in 1912, became one of the principal organisations opposing white minority rule.

## Mandela and the ANC

Mandela was born on 18 July 1918 in Mvezo in the Eastern Cape. He studied at Fort Hare and later moved to Johannesburg, where he became involved in politics and law. In 1944 he helped form the ANC Youth League with Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu and other young activists.

The Youth League called for a more active campaign against racial discrimination. In the 1950s Mandela took part in the Defiance Campaign, which encouraged people to resist unjust laws through organised civil disobedience. He became a prominent national leader, although the state repeatedly restricted his movement and political activity.

After the Sharpeville massacre in March 1960, when police killed 69 people during a protest against pass laws, the government banned the ANC and the Pan Africanist Congress. The banning of organisations and the repression of peaceful protest pushed parts of the liberation movement toward armed resistance.

Mandela helped establish Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK), the ANC's armed wing, in 1961. Its initial campaign focused on sabotage against government installations and infrastructure. Mandela later travelled outside South Africa to seek support and military training. He was arrested in August 1962 and sentenced to five years in prison for leaving the country illegally and inciting workers to strike.

## The Rivonia Trial

While Mandela was already imprisoned, police raided Liliesleaf Farm in Rivonia, near Johannesburg, in July 1963. The farm had been used as a secret headquarters by anti-apartheid activists. Documents found there led to the Rivonia Trial, in which Mandela and other leaders were charged with sabotage and conspiracy to overthrow the government.

On 20 April 1964, Mandela delivered a statement from the dock explaining why the accused had resisted apartheid. He described the democratic ideal for which he was prepared to die. The speech became a defining statement of the struggle, although Mandela was not sentenced to death.

On 12 June 1964, Mandela and several co-accused were sentenced to life imprisonment. He was taken to Robben Island, a prison on an island off Cape Town. His prisoner number was 466/64: the 466th prisoner admitted in 1964.

## Life on Robben Island

Robben Island became a symbol of apartheid repression. Prisoners faced hard labour, strict routines, censorship, limited family visits and deliberate efforts to break their political organisation. Mandela and other political prisoners were separated from ordinary prisoners and subjected to particularly harsh restrictions.

The prison did not end political activity. Mandela and his colleagues debated strategy, studied, taught one another and maintained political relationships. The prison became known among prisoners as a place of learning, even as it remained a site of punishment and isolation.

Mandela's family life was also deeply affected. His mother and eldest son died while he was imprisoned, and he was not allowed to attend their funerals. His marriage to Winnie Mandela was strained by separation, harassment and political pressure.

Mandela spent eighteen years on Robben Island. In 1982 he was transferred to Pollsmoor Prison in Cape Town, along with several senior ANC prisoners. In December 1988, after illness and hospital treatment, he was moved to a house at Victor Verster Prison near Paarl. He spent the final fourteen months of his imprisonment there.

## Pressure for change

By the 1980s, apartheid faced growing resistance inside South Africa and increasing international pressure. Trade unions, student organisations, churches, civic groups and the United Democratic Front helped mobilise opposition. The ANC continued its campaign from exile and through underground networks.

International sanctions, disinvestment campaigns, cultural boycotts and sporting isolation increased the costs of apartheid. South Africa's economy faced serious difficulties, while the government struggled to maintain order through states of emergency and security-force repression.

The government also faced a changing regional environment. The independence of neighbouring states and the conflict in southern Africa made apartheid increasingly difficult to defend. The end of the Cold War reduced some of the international arguments previously used to justify support for the apartheid state.

Negotiations did not begin suddenly in February 1990. There had been secret contacts between Mandela and government representatives for years. Mandela believed that a negotiated settlement was necessary, but he also insisted that the ANC and other liberation organisations had to participate openly and that political prisoners could not be treated as isolated individuals.

In 1985 President P.W. Botha offered Mandela conditional release if he renounced violence. Mandela rejected the offer. A statement read by his daughter Zindzi at a public meeting made clear that he would not accept freedom on terms that left the political rights of the majority unresolved.

## The announcement of 2 February 1990

On 2 February 1990, President F.W. de Klerk addressed Parliament and announced that the ANC, the Pan Africanist Congress and the South African Communist Party would be unbanned. Restrictions on political activity were lifted, and the government announced the release of Mandela.

The announcement was a major turning point. It did not immediately dismantle apartheid laws, and violence and political uncertainty continued. But it made open negotiations possible and allowed organisations that had been forced underground or into exile to operate legally.

Mandela was informed that he would be released. The government initially planned a different release arrangement, but Mandela wanted to leave through the gates of Victor Verster Prison. The date was set for 11 February.

## 11 February: a public return

On the day of his release, crowds gathered outside the prison and along the route to Cape Town. Mandela walked through the gates holding Winnie's hand. He raised his fist, a gesture of resistance and solidarity, and travelled to the city.

At the Grand Parade, he addressed thousands of supporters from the balcony of Cape Town City Hall. He thanked those who had sustained the struggle and called for continued mobilisation. He reaffirmed the goal of a non-racial and democratic South Africa and made clear that the struggle was not over.

The speech mattered because Mandela did not present his release as a personal victory alone. He spoke as a representative of a broad movement and insisted that the demands that had led to his imprisonment remained unresolved.

## Negotiations and a difficult transition

After his release, Mandela travelled widely, meeting supporters and political leaders. In 1991 he was elected president of the ANC, succeeding Oliver Tambo, who had led the organisation during much of Mandela's imprisonment.

Negotiations with the government were difficult. Political violence continued in several parts of the country. The parties disagreed over the constitution, the future of the security forces, the release of political prisoners and the transfer of power. Mandela had to balance pressure from supporters who demanded immediate change with the need to secure a settlement that could be implemented.

The Convention for a Democratic South Africa, known as CODESA, began in December 1991. Negotiations broke down and resumed in different forms. In 1993, after further violence and political crisis, negotiators reached agreement on an interim constitution and a transition to democratic elections.

Mandela and de Klerk were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993 for their work toward the peaceful end of apartheid and the foundations of a new democratic South Africa.

## The election of 1994

On 27 April 1994, South Africans of all races voted in the country's first democratic national election. For many Black South Africans, it was the first time they could vote in a national election. The ANC won a majority, and Mandela was elected president by the new Parliament.

On 10 May 1994, he was inaugurated as South Africa's first democratically elected Black president. The inauguration marked the formal transfer from apartheid rule to a democratic government based on universal adult suffrage.

Mandela's presidency focused on national reconciliation, institution-building and the difficult task of addressing the social and economic inequalities created by apartheid. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was established to investigate human rights violations committed during the apartheid era and provide a public process for testimony and accountability.

Mandela served one term and stepped down in 1999. He continued to work on peace, public health, children's welfare and social development. He died on 5 December 2013.

## What his release meant

Mandela's release did not single-handedly end apartheid. It followed decades of collective action by South Africans and sustained pressure from people and governments around the world. The ANC, other liberation organisations, trade unions, students, community activists, religious leaders and ordinary citizens all contributed to the struggle.

Nor did the end of formal apartheid immediately remove poverty, inequality or racial divisions. South Africa's democratic transition created political rights and new institutions, but the legacies of land dispossession, unequal education and economic exclusion remained.

The significance of 11 February 1990 lies in what it made possible. A man imprisoned for more than twenty-seven years walked free, and a movement that had been banned could return to open politics. The prison gates opened onto negotiations, a democratic election and a new constitutional order. The work of building an equal society, however, continued long after the celebrations.

## Key people

Nelson Mandela: ANC leader imprisoned for 27 years and first democratically elected president of South Africa.

Oliver Tambo: ANC president during much of Mandela's imprisonment and a leading organiser of the movement in exile.

Walter Sisulu: ANC leader and Rivonia Trial defendant who spent many years imprisoned with Mandela.

Winnie Madikizela-Mandela: anti-apartheid activist who sustained political resistance during Mandela's imprisonment.

F.W. de Klerk: South African president who unbanned liberation organisations and negotiated the transition.

Desmond Tutu: Anglican archbishop and anti-apartheid campaigner who later chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

## Timeline

18 July 1918: Nelson Mandela is born in Mvezo, Eastern Cape.

1944: Mandela helps establish the ANC Youth League.

1960: The Sharpeville massacre takes place; the ANC and PAC are banned.

1961: Umkhonto we Sizwe is established.

5 August 1962: Mandela is arrested.

12 June 1964: Mandela and seven co-accused are sentenced to life imprisonment in the Rivonia Trial.

1982: Mandela is transferred from Robben Island to Pollsmoor Prison.

7 December 1988: Mandela is moved to Victor Verster Prison.

2 February 1990: President de Klerk announces the unbanning of the ANC and other organisations.

11 February 1990: Mandela is released from prison.

1991: Mandela is elected president of the ANC.

1993: Mandela and de Klerk receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

27 April 1994: South Africa holds its first democratic national election.

10 May 1994: Mandela is inaugurated as president.

1999: Mandela steps down after one presidential term.

5 December 2013: Mandela dies in Johannesburg.

## Sources

Nelson Mandela Foundation, “Biography of Nelson Mandela” and “Trials and prisons chronology”.

Nelson Mandela Foundation, “Nelson Mandela’s release from prison: 36 years on” (2026).

Government of South Africa, “Life and Times of Mandela”.

Nelson Mandela, Long Walk to Freedom (1994).

fr.title: Nelson Mandela est libéré
fr.text: Nelson Mandela est libéré après 27 ans de prison. Quatre ans plus tard, il devient le premier président de l'Afrique du Sud élu lors d'une élection pleinement démocratique.

ar.title: الإفراج عن نيلسون مانديلا
ar.text: أُفرج عن نيلسون مانديلا بعد 27 عامًا في السجن. وبعد أربع سنوات أصبح أول رئيس لجنوب أفريقيا يُنتخب في انتخابات ديمقراطية شاملة.

ko.title: 넬슨 만델라 석방
ko.text: 넬슨 만델라가 27년간의 수감 생활 끝에 석방되었습니다. 4년 뒤 그는 완전한 민주 선거로 선출된 남아프리카공화국 최초의 대통령이 되었습니다.

ja.title: ネルソン・マンデラが釈放される
ja.text: ネルソン・マンデラが27年間の獄中生活を経て釈放されました。4年後、彼は完全な民主選挙で選ばれた南アフリカ初の大統領となりました。

zh.title: 纳尔逊·曼德拉获释
zh.text: 纳尔逊·曼德拉在狱中度过27年后获释。四年后,他成为南非首位通过全面民主选举产生的总统。

es.title: Nelson Mandela es liberado
es.text: Nelson Mandela fue liberado tras 27 años en prisión. Cuatro años después se convirtió en el primer presidente de Sudáfrica elegido en unas elecciones plenamente democráticas.

sw.title: Nelson Mandela aachiliwa huru
sw.text: Nelson Mandela aliachiliwa huru baada ya miaka 27 gerezani. Miaka minne baadaye akawa Rais wa kwanza wa Afrika Kusini kuchaguliwa katika uchaguzi wa kidemokrasia wa watu wote.
